title: Part 2, Chapter 35
paragraphs: In which the instruction given to Don Quixote about the disenchantment of Dulcinea continues, along with other marvellous incidents

Toward them, to the sound of this agreeable music, came what is called a triumphal car, drawn by six grey mules draped in white linen, and on each mule rode a penitent, also robed in white, carrying a large lighted wax taper in his hand. The car was twice — perhaps three times — the size of the earlier ones, and along its front and sides stood twelve more penitents, all white as snow and all holding lighted tapers: a sight to stir fear as much as wonder. On a raised throne sat a nymph wrapped in a multitude of veils of silver tissue, glittering all over with countless embroidered gold spangles, which made her look, if not richly dressed, at least dazzlingly so. Her face was covered with a thin, transparent silk whose weave did not stop anyone from making out the lovely features of a young woman beneath it, and the many lights made it possible to judge both her beauty and her age, which seemed no less than seventeen and not yet twenty. Beside her sat a figure dressed in what they call a robe of state, reaching to the feet, its head covered with a black veil. But the moment the car drew level with the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote, the music of the clarions stopped, and then the lutes and harps on the car fell silent too; the robed figure rose, flung the garment open, lifted the veil from its face, and revealed plainly the shape of Death itself, fleshless and hideous. At the sight Don Quixote grew uneasy, Sancho was frightened, and even the duke and duchess showed a flicker of alarm. Once on its feet, this living Death began to speak, in a drowsy voice and with a tongue that seemed barely awake:

I am that Merlin of whom the legends tell
that the devil was my father — a lie
that time has only made more believable.
Prince of magic, monarch and treasurer
of the lore of Zoroaster, I watch with a jealous eye
as the present age tries to bury
the gallant deeds of bold knights-errant,
who are, and always have been, dear to my heart.
Enchanters, magicians, and their kind
are mostly hard of heart; I am not.
Mine is a tender heart, soft and compassionate,
and its delight is to do good to everyone.
In the dim caverns of gloomy Dis,
where my soul now dwells, tracing
mystic lines and characters, there reached me
the sorrow-laden cry of the fair one,
the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso.
I knew of her enchantment and her fate,
transformed from high-born lady to peasant girl;
and, moved to pity, I first searched the pages
of countless volumes of my devilish art,
and then, sealing my spirit inside
this grim and ghastly skeleton, I have come here
to reveal where the proper remedy lies
to bring relief in so pitiful a case.
O you, glory and pride of all who wear
the adamantine steel! O shining light,
O beacon, polestar, path, and guide of all
who scorn sleep and the lazy featherbed
to take up the toilsome life of blood-stained arms!
To you, great hero beyond all praise,
La Mancha's splendor and Iberia's star,
Don Quixote, as wise as you are brave — to you I say:
for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso
to recover her original form and beauty,
your squire Sancho must lay
three thousand three hundred lashes
on his own sturdy buttocks, bared to the heavens,
and they must smart and sting and hurt him well.
So those who authored her misfortune have decreed,
and that, ladies and gentlemen, is why I have come.

“By everything that's holy,” Sancho burst out at this, “I'd just as soon give myself three stabs with a dagger as three lashes, never mind three thousand. The devil can take this method of disenchanting! I don't see what my backside has to do with enchantments. By God, if Señor Merlin hasn't found some other way of disenchanting the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, she can go to her grave enchanted.”

“And I'll take you, Don Clown stuffed with garlic,” said Don Quixote, “and tie you to a tree as naked as the day your mother bore you, and give you not three thousand three hundred lashes but six thousand six hundred, laid on so firmly that they won't come off even if you try three thousand three hundred times. And don't answer me a single word, or I'll rip the soul out of you.”

Hearing this, Merlin said, “That will not do, for the lashes the worthy Sancho must receive have to be given of his own free will, not by force, and at whatever time he chooses — no deadline has been set for him. He is also permitted, if he wants to cut the pain of this whipping in half, to have the lashes delivered by another's hand, even if that hand is a somewhat heavy one.”

“No hand shall touch me — not my own, not anyone else's, heavy or weighable,” said Sancho. “Did I give birth to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, that my backside should pay for the sins of her eyes? It's my master who's a part of her — he's forever calling her 'my life' and 'my soul,' his stay and his prop — so he may and should whip himself for her sake and go to all the trouble her disenchantment requires. But me, whip myself? Abernuncio!”

The moment Sancho finished speaking, the silver-clad nymph beside Merlin's ghost rose to her feet, and lifting the thin veil from her face she revealed one that struck everybody as something more than exceedingly beautiful; and with a masculine boldness, in a voice not particularly ladylike, she addressed Sancho directly: “You wretched squire, soul of a water-jug, heart of cork, with bowels of flint and gravel — if they ordered you, you brazen thief, to throw yourself down from some high tower; if they asked you, enemy of the human race, to swallow a dozen toads, two dozen lizards, and three dozen adders; if they wanted you to butcher your wife and children with a sharp and murderous scimitar, nobody would be surprised at your turning stubborn and squeamish. But to make such a fuss over three thousand three hundred lashes — which every poor little charity-boy gets in a month — is enough to amaze, astonish, and stupefy the compassionate hearts of all who hear of it, and of all who will ever come to hear of it in times to come. Turn, you miserable, hard-hearted animal — turn, I say, those skittish owl's eyes of yours on these eyes of mine, which have been compared to radiant stars, and you will see them weeping in trickles and streams, cutting furrows, tracks, and pathways across the fair fields of my cheeks. Let it move you, you cunning, ill-natured monster, that my blooming youth — still in its teens, for I am not yet twenty — is wasting and withering away beneath the husk of a coarse peasant girl; and if I do not appear in that shape right now, it is a special favour Señor Merlin here has granted me, for the sole purpose that my beauty might soften you; for the tears of beauty in distress turn rocks to cotton and tigers to ewes. Lay on to that hide of yours, you great unbroken brute; rouse that lusty energy of yours, which only ever drives you to eat and eat again, and set free the smoothness of my flesh, the gentleness of my nature, and the loveliness of my face. And if you will not relent or see reason for my sake, do it for the sake of that poor knight beside you — your master, I mean — whose soul I can see at this very moment lodged in his throat, not ten fingers' breadth from his lips, waiting only for your harsh or yielding answer either to escape through his mouth or to sink back down into his stomach.”
On hearing this, Don Quixote felt his throat and, turning to the duke, said, “By God, señor, Dulcinea is telling the truth — here is my soul, stuck in my throat like the nut of a crossbow.”
“And what do you say to that, Sancho?” asked the duchess.
“I say, señora,” Sancho answered, “exactly what I said before: as far as the lashes go — abernuncio!”
“Abrenuncio is what you should say, Sancho, not the way you put it,” said the duke.

“Leave me alone, your highness,” said Sancho. “I'm in no mood just now to be fussing over fine points or a letter more or less, because these lashes that are to be given me — or that I'm to give myself — have rattled me so badly I don't know what I'm saying or doing. But what I'd like to know from this lady, my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, is where she learned this way she has of asking for favours. She comes asking me to flay my own flesh with a whip, and she calls me soul of a water-jug and great unbroken brute and a whole string of foul names the devil is welcome to. Is my flesh made of brass? Is it any business of mine whether she's enchanted or not? Does she bring along a basket of fine linen — shirts, kerchiefs, socks (not that I wear any) — to win me over? No, nothing but one insult after another, even though she knows the proverb they use around here, that 'an ass loaded with gold climbs a mountain lightly,' and 'gifts break rocks,' and 'pray to God and keep swinging the hammer,' and 'one “take this” is worth more than two “I'll-give-you's.”' Then there's my master, who ought to be stroking me down and petting me until I turn soft as wool and carded cotton — instead he says that if he gets his hands on me, he'll tie me naked to a tree and double the count of lashes on me. These tender-hearted gentlefolk ought to remember that it's not just a squire they're asking to whip himself, but a governor — as if it were as easy as 'have a drink with your cherries.' Let them learn — plague take them — the proper way to ask, to plead, and to behave; all times are not alike, and people aren't always in a good humour. Right now I'm fit to burst with grief at seeing my green coat torn, and here they come asking me to whip myself of my own free will, when I've as little appetite for it as for turning cacique.”

“Well then, friend Sancho, the plain fact is,” said the duke, “that unless you turn softer than a ripe fig, you will never lay hands on the governorship. A fine thing it would be for me to send my islanders a cruel governor with flinty insides, one who won't bend to the tears of damsels in distress or to the entreaties of wise, commanding, venerable enchanters and sages. In short, Sancho: either you whip yourself, or someone else whips you, or you don't become governor.”
“Señor,” said Sancho, “couldn't I be given two days' grace to think over what's best for me?”

“No, certainly not,” said Merlin. “Here, this minute, on this very spot, the matter must be settled: either Dulcinea goes back to the cave of Montesinos and her former condition as a peasant girl, or in her present form she will be carried off to the Elysian Fields, where she will wait until the full tally of lashes is complete.”

“Come now, Sancho!” said the duchess. “Show some courage, and some gratitude for your master Don Quixote's bread, which you have eaten; we are all bound to serve and please him for his benevolent nature and his lofty deeds of chivalry. Say yes to this whipping, my son; send the devil packing back to the devil, and leave fear to the faint-hearted, for 'a stout heart breaks bad luck,' as you know perfectly well.”

To this Sancho replied with a remark that had nothing to do with the matter at hand; addressing Merlin, he said, “Will your worship tell me one thing, Señor Merlin? When that courier devil rode up, he gave my master a message from Señor Montesinos, telling him to wait for him here, because he was coming to arrange how the lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso was to be disenchanted — but up to now we've seen no Montesinos, nor anything like him.”

To which Merlin answered, “The devil, Sancho, is an ignoramus and a thorough scoundrel. I sent him to find your master with a message from me, not from Montesinos — for Montesinos is in his cave expecting, or more accurately awaiting, his own disenchantment, since there's still the tail of that business left to skin. If he owes you anything, or you have any dealings to settle with him, I'll fetch him and set him down wherever you choose. For the present, make up your mind to accept this penance; believe me, it will do you a great deal of good, for soul as well as body — for your soul, because of the charity with which you'll perform it; for your body, because I know you're of a full-blooded constitution, and drawing off a little blood will do you no harm.”

“The world is full of doctors — even the enchanters turn out to be doctors,” said Sancho. “Still, since everyone keeps telling me the same thing — though I can't see it myself — I declare I'm willing to give myself the three thousand three hundred lashes, on condition that I lay them on whenever I please, with no days or dates fixed; and I'll try to get out of the debt as fast as I can, so the world can enjoy the beauty of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — since it appears, contrary to what I'd thought, that she really is beautiful after all. There must be another condition too: I'm not to be obliged to draw blood with the scourge, and if some of the lashes turn out no harder than fly-swatters, they still count. Item: if I should lose track of the tally, Señor Merlin, who knows everything, is to keep count and let me know how many are still owing or over the number.”

“There will be no need to notify you of any extras,” said Merlin, “because the moment you reach the full number, the lady Dulcinea will be disenchanted then and there, on the very instant, and in her gratitude she will come looking for the worthy Sancho to thank him — and even reward him — for the good deed. So you have no reason to fret about lashes too many or too few; heaven forbid I should cheat anyone out of so much as a hair of his head.”
“Well then, into God's hands with it,” said Sancho. “In this hard spot I find myself in, I give in; I say I accept the penance, on the conditions laid down.”

The instant Sancho spoke these last words, the music of the clarions struck up again and another volley of muskets went off, and Don Quixote threw himself on Sancho's neck, kissing him over and over on the forehead and cheeks. The duke and duchess showed the liveliest satisfaction, the car began to roll on, and as it passed, the fair Dulcinea bowed her head to the duke and duchess and dropped a deep curtsey to Sancho.

And now bright, smiling dawn came hurrying on; the flowers of the field lifted their refreshed heads, and the crystal waters of the brooks, murmuring over the grey and white pebbles, ran to pay their tribute to the rivers that awaited them. The glad earth, the cloudless sky, the fresh breeze, the clear light — each and all gave promise that the day now treading on the skirts of morning would be calm and bright. The duke and duchess, delighted with their hunt and with how cleverly and successfully they had carried out their scheme, returned to their castle resolved to push the joke further; for to them no reality could offer more amusement.
